design_detail: Research letter (JAMA 2015;313(24):2491-2493) reporting a laboratory analysis of commercial products, not of people or cells (the schema has no design for a laboratory analysis of products; 'in-vitro' is the nearest, as for sc_mallock_2024). Purchasers holding a physician's letter, with no history of buying edibles, bought labelled edible cannabis products (baked goods, beverages, candy or chocolate) at nine medical-cannabis dispensaries, three each in San Francisco and Los Angeles (California) and Seattle (Washington), between August and October 2014, within $400 per city: 75 products of 47 brands. Each whole package was homogenized and two samples were tested by high-performance liquid chromatography; measured delta-9-THC and CBD were compared with the label, within 10% counting as accurately labelled. Read together with the correction notice (JAMA 2015;314(2):188, 'Incorrect Labels in Text and in Table 1 Column Headings'), which rewrites two sentences of the Results and gives the column headings of Table 1; where the saved PDF and the correction differ, this card follows the correction.
can_establish: How often the measured THC content of 75 labelled edible products, bought at nine medical-cannabis dispensaries in three US cities in August to October 2014, was within 10% of the label, more than 10% above it or more than 10% below it, and by how much, by city and by product type; how many contained CBD and how often a printed CBD content matched; and the measured content of six cannabinoids per package.
cannot_establish: How accurate edible labels are in other cities or years, in adult-use shops, or under later testing and labelling rules (a non-random sample from 2014 markets that the authors call unregulated, not weighted by sales); how evenly THC was spread between the pieces or servings of a package (whole packages were mixed before testing); whether batches of the same product differ (the number of packages per product is not stated); why products deviated (manufacture, loss in storage, or measurement); and what happens to people who eat these products: no one was given a product, and the Discussion's statements about missing medical benefit and adverse effects are inferences, not measurements.

sample.recruitment: Products, not people. From an Internet directory of dispensaries that listed each one's menu, dispensaries in each city were selected at random until three were found that offered at least one edible product in each of three categories (baked goods, beverages, candy or chocolate) with a label giving at least a specific delta-9-THC content. Between August and October 2014, purchasers with a physician's letter (in line with state law) and no history of buying edibles were sent to these dispensaries to buy as wide a variety of products (type and labelled content) as possible within $400 per city. Purchasers knew the products would be tested, dispensary staff did not, and neither knew the details of the analyses (Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, p. 2491).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Dispensaries: at least one labelled product in each of the three categories, with a specific THC content on the label. Products: chosen by the purchasers for variety within the budget; the number per city reflects what $400 could buy (Table 1, footnote e, p. 2492). Products without a THC label are not described; the Discussion notes that many products carry no cannabinoid content on the label.
sample.demographics: Not applicable (products). The number of purchasers is not stated.
sample.attrition: None reported: all 75 products appear in Table 1.
sample.selection_effects: Not a random sample of products, as the authors state (no source lists all dispensaries, and many products carry no cannabinoid label); medical dispensaries only; three cities; purchases aimed at variety, not at what is most bought; 20 to 32 products per city. Whether the same brand was bought in more than one dispensary or city is not reported. The authors describe these 2014 markets as unregulated.

exposure.measurement: Whole package homogenized (crushed or mixed); two samples (1.5 g of a solid, 25 g of a liquid) tested by high-performance liquid chromatography, averaged and scaled to the total product weight. When the two samples differed by more than 10%, which the paper calls cannabinoid heterogeneity, the entire product was analysed (37 of 75); five randomly chosen products whose duplicates agreed within 10% were also analysed in full and confirmed the duplicate method (Methods, 4th and 5th paragraphs, p. 2491). Six cannabinoids were measured (THC, THCA, CBD, CBDA, CBG, CBN; Table 2, p. 2493). No validation data are given (recovery from chocolate, baked goods or drinks, calibration, limits of quantification), the laboratory that ran the tests is not named, and whether the analysts knew the labels is not stated.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Measured product content, not a dose. Per package (Table 2, p. 2493; median, interquartile range as printed, range): THC 54 mg (99), under 1 to 1,236 mg; THCA 2 (15), under 1 to 173; CBD 2 (3), under 1 to 51; CBDA 1 (5), under 1 to 20; CBG 3 (3), under 1 to 43; CBN 2 (2), under 1 to 20. Labelled THC ranged from 2 to 1,000 mg per package (Table 1, p. 2492). No one consumed the products in the study.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (products). Only six cannabinoids were measured and the results focus on THC and CBD (Methods, 3rd paragraph, p. 2491); other contents (for example solvents, pesticides, microbes or added drugs) were not measured.

comparison.controls: The content printed on each package is the comparator. No reference product, no second laboratory and no comparison with flower or other forms were included.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a product analysis. Not measured or not described: batch-to-batch variation; how long and how products had been stored; whether labels stated content per package or per serving and how per-serving labels were converted; and whether labelled THC was compared with delta-9-THC alone or with THC plus THCA (THCA is reported separately in Table 2, up to 173 mg in one product).

outcomes.instruments: High-performance liquid chromatography (instrument, standards and conditions not given); labels read by the investigators.
outcomes.validity_norms: The 10% limit is described as a basic label-accuracy standard for pharmaceuticals, with no source given. Method validation is limited to the full analysis of five products as a check of the duplicate method.
outcomes.operationalization: As corrected: accurately labelled, measured THC (or CBD) within 10% of the label; underlabelled, more than 10% above the label (the product holds more than it says); overlabelled, more than 10% below the label (it holds less than it says). Deviation is the actual against the labelled amount, in percent (Methods, 5th paragraph, p. 2491; Table 1 footnotes a to d, p. 2492).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not needed: the only test is one chi-squared test of city against the three accuracy categories for THC.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Dispensary staff did not know the products would be tested; the purchasers did. Whether the analysts knew the labels is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: No intervals are given. THC: 13 of 75 (17%) within 10% of the label, 17 (23%) more than 10% above it, 45 (60%) more than 10% below it. Editors' calculation (Wilson 95% intervals): 10.4% to 27.4%, 14.7% to 33.3% and 48.7% to 70.3%; 62 of 75 (82.7%; 72.6% to 89.6%) outside 10%. Mean deviation (SD): within 10%, -3% (4), largest 9%; above, +28% (13), largest +55%; below, -47% (29), largest -99% (Table 1). City: chi-squared 12.94, P = .01; the degrees of freedom are not printed (4 by design); the editors' recomputation from Table 1 gives 12.94 and P = 0.012, with 3 of the 9 expected counts below 5.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned (a research letter).
analysis.selective_reporting: Other cannabinoids were analysed but the results focus on THC and CBD (Table 2 gives their content); accuracy by product type is shown only as counts, without a test; results for single products are not listed.
analysis.power: Not addressed; 20 to 32 products per city and 13 to 40 per product type.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 75 labelled edibles bought at nine medical dispensaries in three US cities in 2014, about one in six held THC within 10% of its label, about one in four held more and about three in five held less, some almost none. The pattern differed by city (as corrected: products holding more THC than labelled were commonest in Los Angeles, products holding less in Seattle). Only 13 products printed a CBD content, and none of them was within 10%.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Discussion says the products failed basic label-accuracy standards for pharmaceuticals (the 10% limit is not sourced) and calls the shortfalls significantly less content, meaning beyond the 10% limit, not a statistical test. Its statements that products with less THC may not give the desired medical benefit and that products with more put patients at risk of adverse effects are inferences resting on two citations (a report of two cases of psychosis after oral cannabis and a viewpoint), not on measurements in people. The authors state the limits plainly (few cities, dispensaries and products; no true random sample; results may not generalize). The main reporting problem is the reversed labels in the text, fixed by the correction: anyone citing the uncorrected text has the city and CBD findings the wrong way round.

timeline.event: Products bought, August to October, at nine medical-cannabis dispensaries in San Francisco, Los Angeles and Seattle.

This research letter (JAMA, 23/30 June 2015). A correction notice (JAMA, 14 July 2015, p. 188) rewrote the Results' sentence on which city had which kind of mislabelling and the sentence on CBD, and gave the column headings of Table 1. The saved PDF carries a note that the article was corrected online on 23 June 2015 to fix labels, yet still prints those two sentences in the form the July correction replaces.

RTI Press overview of edibles cites this letter second-hand: 83 percent of edibles more than 10 percent from the labelled THC, more than half with significantly less and nearly a quarter with more. This agrees with the corrected figures (62 of 75 outside 10%, 82.7%, editors' arithmetic), although the overview calls the measure total THC, a term the letter does not use.

replication.where_it_stands: A single, small, non-random sample of products from 2014. No one has re-tested these products, and later label tests in other markets were not read for this card, so the figures describe what could be bought at these dispensaries then, not edible products in general.

funding.funder: Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, except the cost of the analytical testing, which Werc Shop Laboratories covered. The paper states that neither Johns Hopkins University nor Werc Shop Laboratories had any role in the design or conduct of the study, the data, the manuscript or the decision to submit (Funding/Support and Role of the Funder/Sponsor, p. 2493).
funding.declared_conflicts: Dr Bonn-Miller reported receiving personal fees and nonfinancial support from Tilray (Division of Privateer Holdings) and travel reimbursement from Americans for Safe Access; no other disclosures were reported (p. 2493).
funding.affiliations_note: Four of the six authors are at Werc Shop Laboratory (Pasadena, California: J. C. Raber and M. E. Raber; Bellevue, Washington: Douglass and Miller); Vandrey is at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and Bonn-Miller at the University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine (p. 2491). The author contributions credit two Werc Shop authors (J. Raber and Douglass) with the study's concept and design and with its supervision (p. 2493), which sits uneasily with the statement that Werc Shop Laboratories had no role in the design or conduct. The paper does not describe what Werc Shop Laboratories or Tilray do, and the editors have not added that from other sources.

what_would_settle_it: Repeated, sales-weighted mystery-shopper sampling of edible products in several markets and years, with several packages and batches per product and separate tests of single servings, analysed blind to the label by an independent laboratory that reports its recovery for each food type, would show how often labels match and how evenly THC is spread within a package.

domains.note: Dispensaries chosen at random from a directory, but only those with labelled products in all three categories; products bought for variety within $400 per city, not by sales; medical dispensaries in three cities in 2014. Staff did not know the products would be tested (a strength). Describes what was on offer at these nine dispensaries, not the market.

Duplicate chromatography of the homogenized whole package, with full analysis when duplicates disagreed (37 of 75) and a five-product check of the duplicate method; but no recovery, calibration or quantification-limit data for the food matrices, no named or independent laboratory, and no statement on blinding to the labels. Incomplete extraction from chocolate or baked goods, if present, would push results towards 'less than labelled'; the letter gives no data to judge it.

A clear 10% rule applied to THC and CBD; but whether labels gave content per package or per serving, and how per-serving labels were converted, is not described, nor whether labelled THC was compared with delta-9-THC alone or with THC plus THCA. The text first used the two mislabelling terms the wrong way round in two places (corrected).

Shares reported without intervals; one chi-squared test whose degrees of freedom are not printed and in which 3 of 9 expected counts are below 5 (editors' calculation); products treated as independent although 75 products came from 47 brands and nine dispensaries.

Two Results sentences had the city and CBD findings reversed and were corrected; the saved PDF still prints them reversed. The overall mean shortfall in Table 1 for products below their label (-47%) does not match the city rows (n-weighted -52.5%, editors' arithmetic). The Discussion's inferences about benefit and adverse effects go beyond what was measured but are worded as possibilities.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated risk-of-bias instrument exists for a laboratory analysis of commercial products (METHODS 5.3), so the editors' checklist is used with domains adapted to this design, as for sc_mallock_2024; the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. Once the correction is applied, the THC counts are simple and agree with the table, and buying through unannounced purchasers protects against staff picking products. The concerns are representativeness (nine dispensaries, 2014), unreported method validation, unstated label conventions and the correction history; a second reader may judge measurement validation more severely. Citable for how often the THC and CBD content of these 75 products matched their labels, by city and type; not for the label accuracy of edibles in general or today, for how evenly THC was spread within a package, or for effects in people.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 75 products of 47 brands, bought August to October 2014 at three randomly selected medical-cannabis dispensaries in each of San Francisco (32 products), Los Angeles (20) and Seattle (23), within $400 per city, by purchasers with a physician's letter and no history of buying edibles; dispensary staff did not know the products would be tested. Product types (editors' sums of Table 1): 22 baked goods, 13 beverages, 40 candy or chocolate.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 2491); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 2491); Table 1, products tested and type rows, footnote e (p. 2492)

key_findings.finding: THC against the label, all three cities: 13 of 75 (17%) within 10% (mean deviation -3%, SD 4; largest 9%); 17 (23%) more than 10% above the label (mean +28%, SD 13; largest +55%; measured 34 to 1,236 mg against labelled 20 to 1,000 mg); 45 (60%) more than 10% below (mean -47%, SD 29; largest -99%; measured under 1 to 267 mg against labelled 2 to 325 mg). By type (within / above / below): baked goods 2 / 7 / 13; beverages 3 / 2 / 8; candy or chocolate 8 / 8 / 24.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph, 1st sentence (p. 2491, unchanged by the correction); Table 1, Overall (3 Cities) rows (p. 2492)
key_findings.note: The overall mean for products below their label (-47%) does not match the city rows (-44%, -55% and -61% for 20, 7 and 18 products), whose n-weighted mean is -52.5% (editors' arithmetic); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: By city, within 10% / more than 10% above / more than 10% below: San Francisco 8 (25%) / 4 (13%) / 20 (62%) of 32; Los Angeles 4 (20%) / 9 (45%) / 7 (35%) of 20; Seattle 1 (4%) / 4 (17%) / 18 (78%) of 23; chi-squared 12.94, P = .01. As corrected, products holding more THC than labelled were likeliest in Los Angeles and products holding less in Seattle.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, city rows (p. 2492); Results, 1st paragraph, 2nd sentence as corrected (JAMA 2015;314(2):188)

key_findings.finding: CBD: 44 of 75 products (59%) had detectable CBD but only 13 printed a CBD content; as corrected, 4 held more than 10% more CBD than labelled and 9 more than 10% less, so none of the 13 was within 10% (editors' arithmetic: 4 + 9 = 13). Median THC:CBD ratio among products with detectable CBD 36:1; 7 had ratios below 10:1 and 1 a 1:1 ratio. Content of cannabinoids other than THC was generally low.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (3rd sentence as corrected, JAMA 2015;314(2):188); Table 2 (p. 2493)

key_findings.finding: Measured content per product (measured product content, not doses), mg, median (interquartile range as printed) and range: THC 54 (99), under 1 to 1,236; THCA 2 (15), under 1 to 173; CBD 2 (3), under 1 to 51; CBDA 1 (5), under 1 to 20; CBG 3 (3), under 1 to 43; CBN 2 (2), under 1 to 20.
key_findings.note: The interquartile range is printed as a single number, apparently its width; medians are given because the values were not normally distributed.

key_findings.finding: Testing: whole packages homogenized, two samples tested by high-performance liquid chromatography, averaged and scaled to the product's total weight; duplicates differed by more than 10% (called cannabinoid heterogeneity) in 37 products, which were then analysed in full; five randomly chosen products whose duplicates agreed were also analysed in full and confirmed the duplicate method. Rule: within 10% of the label, accurate; more than 10% above, underlabelled; more than 10% below, overlabelled. Location effect tested by chi-squared, P < .05 two-sided.

Authors' reading: products from three large cities, though unregulated, failed basic label-accuracy standards for pharmaceuticals; more than half held significantly less cannabinoid than labelled, some negligible THC, and may not give the desired medical benefit; others held significantly more THC than labelled, putting patients at risk of adverse effects (two citations); regulation and quality assurance are needed. Limits stated: few cities, dispensaries and products; no source lists all dispensaries and many products lack a cannabinoid label, so a true random sample was not possible and the results may not generalize.

Correction notice: the Results should read that underlabelled products were likeliest in Los Angeles and overlabelled products in Seattle (chi-squared 12.94, P = .01), and that 4 products were underlabelled and 9 overlabelled for CBD; the third column of Table 1 is headed Underlabelled (footnote b) and the fourth Overlabelled (footnote c). The overall shares (17%, 23%, 60%) are as in the saved PDF.
key_findings.locator: JAMA 2015;314(2):188, Correction, 'Incorrect Labels in Text and in Table 1 Column Headings' (right column)

key_findings.finding: Funding and ties as printed: Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine funded the project except the cost of analytical testing, covered by Werc Shop Laboratories; neither had a role in the design, conduct, data, manuscript or decision to submit. Four of six authors at Werc Shop Laboratory; concept and design credited to Vandrey, J. Raber, Douglass and Bonn-Miller, supervision to Vandrey, J. Raber and Douglass. Bonn-Miller: personal fees and nonfinancial support from Tilray (Division of Privateer Holdings), travel reimbursement from Americans for Safe Access.
key_findings.locator: Author Affiliations (p. 2491); Author Contributions, Conflict of Interest Disclosures, Funding/Support, Role of the Funder/Sponsor (p. 2493)

reporting_issues.issue: The saved PDF (downloaded 23 June 2015, with a note that the article was corrected on 23 June 2015 to fix labels in the text and in Table 1) still says overlabelled products were likeliest in Los Angeles and underlabelled in Seattle, which contradicts its own Table 1 (Los Angeles 45% above the label; Seattle 78% below). The July 2015 correction reverses the sentence to match the table.
reporting_issues.consequence: Follow the correction, which agrees with Table 1. Any source repeating the uncorrected sentence has the city finding the wrong way round.

reporting_issues.issue: The CBD sentence in the saved PDF says 4 products were overlabelled and 9 underlabelled; the correction says 4 underlabelled and 9 overlabelled.
reporting_issues.consequence: Under the corrected wording, 9 of the 13 products with a CBD label held less CBD than stated and 4 held more; none was within 10%.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1, the overall mean deviation for products below their label is -47% (SD 29), but the city rows (-44%, n = 20; -55%, n = 7; -61%, n = 18) give an n-weighted mean of -52.5% (editors' arithmetic). The same check reproduces the overall means for accurate (-2.8%, printed -3%) and above-label products (+27.7%, printed +28%). The correction does not mention it.
reporting_issues.consequence: The typical shortfall is about half of the labelled THC either way; cite the overall -47% with a note that the city rows imply about -53%.

reporting_issues.issue: The chi-squared test is printed without its degrees of freedom; 3 of the 9 expected counts are below 5 (editors' calculation from Table 1), and products are treated as independent although they came from 47 brands and nine dispensaries.
reporting_issues.consequence: The city difference is suggestive rather than firm; the P value is approximate.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion's 'significantly less' and 'significantly more' content means beyond the 10% limit; no per-product test or measurement uncertainty is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Products close to the 10% limit may be misclassified by measurement error; the large deviations are not affected.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter does not say whether labels gave content per package or per serving, or whether labelled THC was compared with delta-9-THC alone or with THC plus THCA; the 2016 overview citing it calls the measure total THC.
reporting_issues.consequence: What counts as accurate rests on conventions the letter does not spell out; this matters most for products with a per-serving label or with much THCA.
